answers.B: Extremely lax brain
answers.C: Restricted exposure of the sylvian cistern
answers.D: Wide roomy exposure of the sylvian cistern
answers.E: Satisfactory exposure of surrounded arteries for temporary occlusion

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Mycotic aneurysms came to describe all aneurysms of infectious origin.
answers.B: Intracranial aneurysms of infectious etiology are rare and represent approximately 2–6 % of all intracranial aneurysms.
answers.C: The incidence may be higher in children.
answers.D: Fungal or “true” mycotic aneurysms are rare.
answers.E: The incidence of these lesions has recently decreased.

questions.explanation: Fungal or “true” mycotic aneurysms are rare. However, the incidence of these lesions has recently increased as a result of more patients with immunocompromised states. The incidence may be higher in children, in whom they account for as many as 10 % of all intracranial aneurysms.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: These are typically friable lesions.
answers.B: Can be divided into intravascular and extravascular origin of infection.
answers.C: These from extravascular source such as meningitis tend to occur proximally.
answers.D: These from extravascular source such as meningitis tend to occur distally.
answers.E: Embolic infectious aneurysms associated with infective endocarditis occur predominantly in distal cerebral arterial regions.

questions.explanation: These are typically friable lesions and often not separable from the surrounding parenchyma, which plays an important role in surgical planning.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms Intravascular infection, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Intravascularly infectious aneurysms are bacterial but may rarely be fungal.
answers.B: Intravascularly infectious aneurysms tend to form in branch points in the distal vasculature.
answers.C: The most common location is the DACA.
answers.D: Infectious aneurysms are most commonly from mitral valve septic vegetations.
answers.E: Numerous emboli cause multiple aneurysms in as many as 30 % of patients.

questions.explanation: The most common location is the distal MCA. Because of their embolic etiology, intravascularly derived infectious aneurysms tend to form in locations where blood flow is maximal, and the vascular anatomy favors the lodging of embolic particles, such as vessel branch points in the distal vasculature. This contrasts with classic berry aneurysms, which tend to form on large basal vessels as solitary lesions. The most common location is the distal MCA, where more than 60 % of emboli lodge.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Endocarditis, particularly left-sided valve disease, predisposes patient to infectious aneurysms and neurological complications.
answers.B: 80 % of intracranial infectious aneurysms are due to endocarditis.
answers.C: 20–40 % of patients with endocarditis suffer neurological sequelae.
answers.D: Cerebral infarction is the least common.
answers.E: Intracranial hemorrhage occurs in 5 %.

questions.explanation: Cerebral infarction is most common and affects up to 31 % of patients. Overall, in 1–4 % of patients with infective endocarditis, an infectious intracranial aneurysm is clinically diagnosed.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms (extravascular) The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Extravascular infection can extend into the arterial wall and induce arteritis.
answers.B: The most common location for extravascular infection is the MCA.
answers.C: Streptococcus viridans and Staphylococcus aureus are most common.
answers.D: Multiple organisms are found in less than 5 % of patients.
answers.E: Despite multiple blood or CSF cultures, 20 % fail to grow an organism.

questions.explanation: Usual locations include the intracavernous ICA, the midbasilar artery, and the vertebral artery. Extravascular infection such as meningitis can potentially extend into the arterial wall and induce arteritis and aneurysm formation. Extravascular infection such as meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis, cerebral abscess, subdural empyema, osteomyelitis of the skull, tonsillitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis, and wound infection, as well as drug abuse, can potentially extend into the arterial wall and induce arteritis and aneurysm formation. Streptococcus viridans and Staphylococcus aureus are responsible for 57–90 % of infectious intracranial aneurysms. Despite multiple blood or CSF cultures, at least 12–20 % of patients fail to grow an organism.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms FUNGAL, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Most fungal aneurysms find their origin in the extravascular space.
answers.B: These “true” mycotic aneurysms are smaller and more saccular in shape.
answers.C: Aspergillus is the most common fungus cultured.
answers.D: The tendency of Aspergillus for intramural growth is directly related to the fusiform shape seen with fungal aneurysms.
answers.E: Aspergillosis of the CNS is usually from direct infection of paranasal sinuses.

questions.explanation: These “true” mycotic aneurysms tend to be larger and more fusiform in shape with a higher association of occlusion of the vessel than occurs with bacterial aneurysms. Aspergillus is the most common fungus cultured, followed by Phycomycetes and Candida albicans. Aneurysms of fungal etiology usually occur in immunocompromised hosts. Direct spread of a fungal infection associated with an aneurysm after craniofacial and other neurosurgical procedures has also been described. Aspergillosis of the CNS is usually from direct infection via the paranasal sinus or indirectly by hematogenous spread (lungs).

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The most common manifestation is a focal neurological deficit.
answers.B: Focal neurological deficit occurred in about 50 % of patients.
answers.C: Majority of neurological manifestations in patients with endocarditis are due to an infectious aneurysm.
answers.D: Rheumatic heart disease and related valvular abnormalities are important predisposing factor.
answers.E: Prosthetic valves and intravenous drug abuse have become important predisposing factors.

questions.explanation: Neurological manifestations are common in patients with endocarditis, with only a minority ultimately referable to an infectious aneurysm. The most common manifestation is a focal neurological deficit, which occurred in 48 % of patients in one larger series. This finding is in contrast to other intracranial aneurysms, which are much less likely to be accompanied by focal signs or symptoms. Prosthetic valves, elderly sclerotic valve disease, and nosocomially acquired bloodstream infections and intravenous drug abuse have become the most important predisposing factors.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The mortality associated with infectious aneurysms is highly variable, ranging from 12 % to as high as 80 %.
answers.B: Most important prognostic factor for outcome is the presence of ischemia.
answers.C: Intracranial hemorrhage in the setting of endocarditis is a strong indication for cerebral angiography.
answers.D: Intracranial fungal aneurysms impart an even worse prognosis.
answers.E: Intracranial fungal aneurysms mortality rate is greater than 90 % despite medical or surgical therapy.

questions.explanation: The most important prognostic factor for outcome is the presence of hemorrhage. CSF cultures in patients with intracranial aneurysms of infectious etiology will often fail to grow an organism, with one study finding CSF cultures positive in just 16 % of patients.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms Indications for conservative management, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Unruptured aneurysms.
answers.B: Aneurysm arising from the proximal cerebral vessels and sacrifice of the parent artery is not possible.
answers.C: Surgical obliteration of aneurysms results in serious neurological deficits.
answers.D: Progression of aneurysms while undergoing antibiotic therapy.
answers.E: Fungal aneurysms.

questions.explanation: Regression of aneurysms while undergoing antibiotic therapy. Neurological complications can develop in up to 30 % of patients after the initiation of antibiotic therapy. Consequently, follow-up angiography is important to monitor intracranial infectious aneurysms during antibiotic treatment, and aneurysmal growth should prompt urgent surgical treatment.

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms Indications for surgical intervention, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The presence of symptomatic mass effect from a hematoma or the aneurysm
answers.B: An unruptured aneurysm
answers.C: Enlargement of an aneurysm during appropriate antibiotic treatment
answers.D: Failure of an aneurysm to resolve despite a full course of appropriate antibiotic therapy
answers.E: Neurological deterioration during antibiotic therapy

questions.explanation: Ruptured aneurysm

questions.question: Infectious intracranial aneurysms* The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Whenever possible, a short course of antibiotics should be given to allow reparative fibrosis of the aneurysm.
answers.B: Clipping is very effective if the aneurysm is friable in nature and adherence to surrounding parenchyma.
answers.C: Excision of the aneurysm with a short segment of parent vessel is a potent treatment option but can be performed only in distal non-eloquent vessel.
answers.D: In patients who cannot tolerate endovascular occlusion of the parent vessel, surgery should be planned.
answers.E: In those patients, surgical options include potential bypass, reanastomosis, or sparing of the parent artery.

questions.explanation: Clipping is frequently not possible if the aneurysm is friable nature and adherence to surrounding parenchyma.

questions.question: Neoplastic intracranial aneurysms* The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The classic cause is cardiac myxoma.
answers.B: Cardiac myxoma usually involves the left atrium and tumor emboli are carried to cranial arteries.
answers.C: The commonest site is the ICA.
answers.D: Metastatic choriocarcinoma may also cause aneurysms.
answers.E: Rarely, local spread by tumors at the skull base and invasion of the arterial wall causes an aneurysm.

questions.explanation: The commonest sites are branches of the MCA, and aneurysms are either fusiform or saccular in shape and often multiple. A rare type of aneurysm is usually caused by intravascular metastasis rather than arterial wall invasion by tumor. Metastatic choriocarcinoma may also invade intracranial arteries and cause arterial rupture, occlusion, or aneurysms by disrupting the internal elastic laminar and media.

questions.question: Multiple intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Incidence of multiple aneurysms is 15–20 %.
answers.B: In patients with multiple aneurysms, the most common site is DACA.
answers.C: In patients with multiple aneurysms, the second most common site is MCA.
answers.D: Bilateral symmetrical aneurysms (mirror aneurysms) may occur.
answers.E: In the setting of an aneurysmal SAH, the risk for subsequent rupture of additional incidental aneurysms is significantly higher.

questions.explanation: In patients with multiple aneurysms, the most common sites are ICA and MCA.

questions.question: Multiple intracranial aneurysms Risk factors, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Hypertension, smoking, and female gender (especially postmenopausal women) are significant risk factors.
answers.B: Sickle cell disease.
answers.C: Polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Marfan’s syndrome.
answers.D: 1 % of AVM-associated aneurysms are multiple.
answers.E: Patients with familial aneurysms and multiple aneurysms tend to be younger.

questions.explanation: 40–50 % of AVM-associated aneurysms are multiple. Most of these aneurysms being located on the feeding vessel of the AVM (85 %). Hypertension found to be most important one associated with multiplicity. Patients with familial aneurysms and multiple aneurysms tend to be younger, and there is a higher incidence of MCA and ICA. 57 % of sickle cell disease had more than one aneurysm. Rare cases of hereditary connective tissue diseases, such as polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, and Marfan’s syndrome are also risk factors.

questions.question: Multiple intracranial aneurysms* Prediction of rupture site: When a patient present with SAH and is found to have multiple aneurysms, the following may be clues as to which aneurysm has bled; the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Epicenter (center of greatest concentration) of blood on CT or MRI.
answers.B: In MRI, focal edema or increased signal adjacent to one aneurysm may indicate a recent hemorrhage.
answers.C: In angiography, aneurysm bleb, irregular contour (“Murphy’s tit”) signs.
answers.D: Focal vasospasm, changing aneurysm shape in serial angiograms, and extravasation of contrast.
answers.E: If none of the above help, then suspect the smallest aneurysm is the source.

questions.explanation: If none of the above help, then suspect the largest aneurysm is the source. Other assisting points: history, clinical exam, EEG, and isotope scan (rapid flow suggests perfusion; static flow suggests infarct). False localization of the ruptured site may result in disastrous postoperative hemorrhage from the unprotected ruptured aneurysm. The most common cause of post-op bleeding was felt to be from rebleeding of the original aneurysm which ruptured that was missed on initial angiogram.

questions.question: Revascularization techniques for complex aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Indicated if atherosclerosis of the aneurysm neck or the parent artery can make clipping dangerous or impossible.
answers.B: Indicated if recurrent aneurysms after endovascular coil embolization may be unclippable.
answers.C: Treatment options include clip occlusion of the aneurysm along with the branching vessel or vessels, parent artery Hunterian ligation, and trapping.
answers.D: All proximal vessel occlusion often results in ischemia, and therefore bypass should be considered.
answers.E: Even if the patient passes a balloon test occlusion, there remains up to a 20 % chance of stroke with complete occlusion without a bypass.

questions.explanation: Proximal vessel occlusion (ICA or vertebral artery) may be tolerated without bypass. Occlusion of branches such as the MCA, AICA, and PICA often result in ischemia, and therefore bypass should be considered. Preoperative evaluation by angiography and balloon test occlusion (with or without hypotensive provocative testing or cerebral blood flow measurements) may aid in the identification of patients who can tolerate carotid sacrifice.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms Bypass types, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type I bypass: interposition vein grafts
answers.B: Type II bypass: extracranial-to-intracranial bypass with a saphenous vein or radial artery graft
answers.C: Type III bypass: scalp artery (STA or occipital) extracranial-to-intracranial bypass
answers.D: Type IV bypass: extracranial-to-intracranial bypass
answers.E: Type IV bypass: direct intracranial revascularization

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Type I bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type I bypass involves an interposition graft from the parent artery proximal to the site of occlusion to the point immediately distal to the parent artery.
answers.B: The primary example is the purely intracranial petrous carotid-to-supraclinoid carotid saphenous vein interposition graft.
answers.C: The most important disadvantage is that it requires prolonged occlusion of ECA.
answers.D: Being technically complex and requiring a lengthy procedure are also disadvantages.
answers.E: It is associated with a significant complication rate related to graft occlusion and perioperative ischemic brain injury.

questions.explanation: The most important disadvantage is that it requires a prolonged period of ICA occlusion.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Type II bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type II bypass consists of a saphenous vein interposition graft between the extracranial carotid artery and a major intracranial branch vessel.
answers.B: This procedure is used when major arterial trunk must be occluded to treat tumor or giant aneurysm and distal collateral circulation is inadequate.
answers.C: A vein graft generally has higher long-term patency.
answers.D: A vein graft has higher risk of kinking and caliber mismatch.
answers.E: A type II bypass can be a substitute for an STA-MCA bypass when the scalp artery is hypoplastic or occluded.

questions.explanation: A vein graft generally has lower long-term patency, higher risk of kinking, and caliber mismatch between the larger vein and smaller intracranial vessels. Type II bypasses: extracranial-to-intracranial bypass with a saphenous vein graft or radial artery graft.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Type III bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Is extracranial-to-intracranial bypass via scalp artery (superficial temporal or occipital).
answers.B: This procedure is performed when a giant aneurysm requires occlusion of a single, crucial arterial branch.
answers.C: This procedure is performed when carotid occlusion is required and the circle of Willis is only marginally inadequate.
answers.D: The STA is used to revascularize the MCA territory only.
answers.E: The occipital artery is most commonly used for bypass to the PICA, but it can also be used to revascularize the AICA as well.

questions.explanation: The STA can be used to revascularize the MCA territory, as well as the distal posterior circulation via the superior cerebellar artery or PCA. Pedicled scalp artery is used as the donor vessel.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Type IV bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Is direct intracranial revascularization.
answers.B: Involves an anastomosis between two adjacent cerebral arteries.
answers.C: This type of procedure can involve end-to-end primary reanastomosis after excision of an aneurysm.
answers.D: Examples include PICA-PICA and pericallosal-pericallosal anastomoses.
answers.E: Examples do not include MCA-MCA and PICA-AICA anastomoses.

questions.explanation: Examples include PICA-PICA, pericallosal-pericallosal, MCA-MCA, and PICA-AICA anastomoses. This type of procedure can involve end-to-end primary reanastomosis after excision of an aneurysm, side-to-side anastomosis of two adjacent intracranial arteries, or an end-to side anastomosis between two cerebral arteries. Pericallosal-to-pericallosal bypass can be used to treat fusiform aneurysms of the proximal pericallosal artery or for giant anterior communicating artery aneurysms that require trapping. This side-to-side anastomosis serves as a new communicating artery. A PICA-to-PICA anastomosis can be used when the occipital artery is small or has been damaged during a previous surgical procedure.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Normal blood flow of the MCA is about 250 mL/min.
answers.B: Blood flow of saphenous vein graft is 70–140 mL/min.
answers.C: Blood flow of radial artery graft is 40 and 70 mL/min.
answers.D: Blood flow of STA graft is 15–30 mL/min.
answers.E: Average diameter of radial artery graft is larger than saphenous vein graft.

questions.explanation: Radial artery graft can be used, which has a smaller diameter (about 3.5 mm) and a flow rate between 40 and 70 mL/min. Blood flow through a saphenous vein graft, which averages about 4–5 mm in diameter, is high enough to support the circulation in an entire major arterial territory at a level well above the ischemic threshold. Blood flow of saphenous vein graft typically ranges from 70 to 140 mL/ min and can exceed 250 mL/min.

questions.question: Revascularization procedures for complex aneurysms* Bypass, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: In saphenous vein graft, it is a must to reverse the ends, so that the distal end in the leg will be the intracranial end.
answers.B: The ideal arterial recipient site of MCA is M2 or M3 (free of perforating vessels).
answers.C: STA-MCA bypass includes a craniotomy centered 6 cm above the external auditory meatus (Chater’s point), where several large MCA branches emerge from the distal sylvian fissure.
answers.D: The most serious acute complication is early graft occlusion.
answers.E: If there is any doubt about the integrity of the graft, intraoperative angiography should be considered.

questions.explanation: It is also important to pass the saphenous vein so that the end that was proximal in the leg is the end used for the cranial, distal anastomosis (because of the unidirectional valve arrangement). The most serious acute complication is early graft occlusion. Rate of ischemic complications and graft occlusion typically exceeds 10 %. A normal flow signal should be confirmed with intraoperative Doppler assessment. Subdural or epidural hematomas (or both) developed postoperatively. Some of these hematomas were small and asymptomatic.

Further classification of these complex surgical cases of inadequately embolized aneurysms was attempted. Group A (65 % of cases) allowed direct surgical clipping. Group B (23 % of cases) showed parent vessel narrowing after clip application, which required extraction of coils from the fundus and reconstruction of the neck by clip or suture. Group C (12 % of cases) consisted of emergency coil removal after embolization procedures.

questions.question: Traumatic intracranial aneurysms (TICA) The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Despite the common occurrence of head trauma, TICA are rare entities that represent less than 1 % of all intracranial aneurysms.
answers.B: 20 % of TICA are multiple.
answers.C: TICA occur relatively frequently in children.
answers.D: All TICA have a propensity to bleed at the time of initial trauma.
answers.E: The anterior circulation is most often affected, with peripheral branches of the MCA being the most frequent site, followed by pericallosal vessels.

questions.explanation: ICA have a propensity to bleed weeks after the initial trauma. Each individual aneurysm may regress, enlarge, or form in delayed fashion. In aneurysms involving the peripheral vascular tree, there is delayed neurological deterioration, usually within 3 weeks of the injury.

questions.question: TICA The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The term pseudoaneurysm is often used to describe aneurysms related to trauma.
answers.B: Pseudoaneurysms, which form the majority of TICA, are essentially contained hematomas with disruption of all three layers of the vessel wall.
answers.C: True aneurysm and a false one are always possible to distinguish them on angiography.
answers.D: Distinction between a true aneurysm and a false one requires histologic analysis.
answers.E: TICA occur distally in the vascular tree, and this peripheral location reflects the underlying mechanism of injury.

questions.explanation: True aneurysm and a false one are not always possible to distinguish them on angiography.

questions.question: TICA MECHANISM, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The relative incidence of TICA varies according to etiology.
answers.B: TICA may be the result of either penetrating or nonpenetrating trauma.
answers.C: Aneurysm formation being much less likely after closed head injury than after penetrating trauma.
answers.D: Aneurysm formation being less likely after low-velocity than after high-velocity penetrating injuries.
answers.E: TICA have been reported to occur iatrogenically, such as after transsphenoidal surgery and endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

questions.explanation: Aneurysm formation being much more likely after low-velocity penetrating injuries (as knives, screwdrivers) than after high-velocity penetrating injuries caused by missiles. The relative incidence of TICA varies according to etiology: blunt trauma in 70 %, penetrating injuries in 20 %, and iatrogenic in about 10 %. In addition to their occurrence after traditional trauma, TICA have been reported to occur iatrogenically, such as after transsphenoidal surgery, sinus surgery, ventricular taps, stereotactic brain biopsy, and endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

questions.question: TICA MECHANISM, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: TICA are 14 times more likely with shrapnel injuries than with bullet injuries, which are of higher velocity.

answers.C: With respect to missile injuries, aneurysm formation in 0.1–8 % of patients sustaining this type of injury.
answers.D: The MCA are most at risk when fractures involve the skull base.
answers.E: Penetrating missile injuries usually affect the supratentorial vessels.

questions.explanation: The petrous and cavernous portions of the ICA are most at risk when fractures involve the skull base.

answers.A: Severe and life-threatening epistaxis can be the initial event in MCA injury.
answers.B: Because most TICA are false aneurysms, ICH is often the reason for this deterioration.
answers.C: Penetrating trauma is often associated with ICH.
answers.D: After missile injuries, concomitant ICH is found in up to 80 % of patients.
answers.E: In low-velocity penetrating injuries, 50 % of patients had an ICH.

questions.question: TICA MECHANISM, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Cerebral angiography is the “gold standard” and should be performed in all cases of penetrating trauma.
answers.B: Angiography is particularly important in patients with orbitopterional injuries, penetrating fragments, and SAH, ICH, or SDH.
answers.C: In penetrating trauma, traumatic aneurysms may be visualized on angiography as early as 2 h after the injury.
answers.D: In penetrating trauma, the majority of aneurysms are angiographically apparent in the first day.
answers.E: Once a traumatic aneurysm has been diagnosed, therapy should be instituted.

questions.explanation: In penetrating trauma, the majority of aneurysms are angiographically apparent in 2–3 weeks.

questions.question: TICA MANAGEMENT, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Surgery is still the mainstay of treatment.
answers.B: Endovascular therapy is becoming an important option, particularly those involving the skull base.
answers.C: TICA may be amenable to either resection or bypass and wrapping.
answers.D: The outcome is related more to the aneurysm itself than to the primary injury.
answers.E: TICA have a mortality rate of 30 %.

questions.explanation: The outcome is related more to the primary injury than to the aneurysm itself. Endovascular therapy has not been a mainstay of treatment of TICA in the peripheral vascular tree because of the high incidence of false aneurysms and the risk for rupture.

questions.question: ACP (anterior clinoid process) drilling during approaches for various intracranial aneurysm The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Anatomically ACP, formed by the medial extension of the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, provides a bony roof to the superior orbital fissure (SOF) and the anterior cavernous sinus.
answers.B: The optic strut extends from the inferomedial surface of the ACP to the body of the sphenoid bone, separating the optic canal from the SOF.
answers.C: The ACP is thus connected to the skull at two main points of bony fixation: the medial aspect of the lesser sphenoid wing and the optic strut.
answers.D: The ACP and optic strut define and obstruct access to the anterior and lateral borders of the ascending ICA.
answers.E: The superomedial portion of the ACP is connected to the planum sphenoidale by the roof of the optic canal, the most posterior portion of which is formed by a dural fold called the falciform ligament.

questions.explanation: The ACP is thus connected to the skull at three main points of bony fixation: the medial aspect of the lesser sphenoid wing, the optic strut, and the roof of the optic canal.

questions.question: ACP drilling* during skull base approaches for various intracranial aneurysms The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The direction of the drilling is from lateral to medial.
answers.B: The optic strut is drilled and the clinoid process freed from its bony fixation points.
answers.C: During ACP drilling, orbitomeningeal artery bleeding indicates proximity to the SOF.
answers.D: Venous bleeding from the lateral cavernous sinus wall is common during the procedure and generally responds to tamponade and pressures them by Surgicel or Gelfoam.
answers.E: Thermal injury can occur during drilling of the ACP and is prevented by generous irrigation to dissipate the heat or by using the newer ultrasonic bone aspirators.

questions.question: Fusiform aneurysm (FA) DEFINITION, the FALSE answer is:

questions.explanation: Fusiform aneurysms are characterized by circumferential involvement of the parent artery, the absence of a defined neck, and a longish course. The spectrum of fusiform aneurysms may arise from congenital, acquired, or iatrogenic defects in the vessel wall, with or without atherosclerosis, and hypertension, or may develop after intimal tear from dissection. Distinct subgroups of fusiform aneurysms are serpentine aneurysms, large and partially thrombosed tortuous aneurysms with a central parent channel, eccentrically located within the intraluminal clot. This channel is not endothelialized and does not contain elastic lamina or media. The etiology of serpentine aneurysms is still totally unclear. They may develop from a degenerative form of atherosclerosis, infection, or may be congenital. They occur most commonly in the internal carotid artery, the middle cerebral artery, and posterior cerebral artery. Typically, they present with symptoms of mass effect. Subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage is rare.

questions.explanation: Small AVMs tend to present more often as hemorrhages than do large ones. The incidence of first bleed for unruptured AVM or the annual rebleed rate or lifelong risk of bleeding per year is 2–4 %, while the risk of rebleed from an AVM in the first year is as high as 5–15 %. Because of the higher pressures in the feeding artery, it was postulated that larger AVMs presented as seizure more often simply because their size made them more likely to involve the cortex. The combined annual morbidity plus mortality from AVMs is approximately 2 %, the annual mortality rate is 1 %, the mortality at each bleed is 10 %, and the morbidity for each bleed is 30 to 50 %. About statement E, the exact mechanisms involved in spontaneous AVM regression are uncertain but the most common is compression of the lesion (leading to acute intravascular thrombosis) from intracranial hemorrhage. Several factors appear to be associated with spontaneous occlusion of cerebral AVM: single draining vein (84 % of cases of spontaneous occlusion), solitary arterial feeder (30 %), and small size of the nidus (<3 cm in 50 %).

answers.A: The most frequent sites for DAVFs are the transverse and sigmoid sinus, anterior cranial base, and tentorium.
answers.B: The transverse/sigmoid location is the most common site.
answers.C: Carotid-cavernous and transverse/sigmoid DAVFs are more common in women.
answers.D: Anterior fossa and tentorial DAVFs are more common in men.
answers.E: Usually found adjacent to dural venous sinuses and more in right side.

questions.explanation: Usually found adjacent to dural venous sinuses. Most common transverse sinus (63 %) and more in left side (usually at the transverse and sigmoid junction). The transverse/sigmoid location is the most common and represents more than 50 % of DAVFs.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: DAVFs consist of a nidus of arteriovenous shunting within the leaflets of the dura mater, in proximity or continuity to a major dural venous sinus or cortical vein.
answers.B: These fistulas are frequently congenital.
answers.C: Grossly, the dural arteries are thickened and the veins dilated in an abnormal vascular network within the wall of a venous sinus.
answers.D: Fistulas may be high or low flow.
answers.E: Fistulas may have unilateral or bilateral supply.

questions.explanation: These fistulas are frequently idiopathic but can be acquired causes like venous thrombosis, trauma, tumor, cranial surgery, sinus infection or meningitis, or association with meningiomas. Demyelination may be seen around leptomeningeal veins as a result of venous hypertension which can lead to leptomeningeal retrograde drainage and predispose these channels to become varicose and potentially rupture.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Natural history, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: DAVFs are classified as high or low risk based on the pattern of venous drainage.
answers.B: DAVFs with retrograde drainage or cortical venous drainage are typically considered to be associated less frequently with ICH.
answers.C: Untreated DAVFs have an annual hemorrhage rate of 1.6 %.
answers.D: Persistence of cortical venous reflux in intracranial DAVFs carries an annual risk for neurological deficits of 15 %.
answers.E: Persistence of cortical venous reflux in intracranial DAVFs carries an annual mortality rate of 10 %.

questions.explanation: DAVFs with retrograde drainage or cortical venous drainage are typically considered to be associated more frequently with ICH, thus warranting more aggressive treatment.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Natural history (risk factors for hemorrhage), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Cortical venous drainage
answers.B: Focal neurological deficits
answers.C: DAVFs located in the anterior fossa
answers.D: Male sex
answers.E: Increasing age

questions.explanation: DAVFs located in the posterior fossa are a risk factor for hemorrhage, not the anterior fossa. Five risk factors for hemorrhage are cortical venous drainage, focal neurological deficits, DAVFs located in the posterior fossa, male sex, and increasing age.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Clinical features, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Patients with DAVFs are frequently asymptomatic.
answers.B: The most common initial symptoms are pulse-synchronous tinnitus and headache.
answers.C: Tinnitus is frequent with carotid-cavernous DAVFs.
answers.D: DAVFs can be accompanied by ICH, seizures, and focal neurological deficits, similar to pial AVMs.
answers.E: Intracranial hemorrhage as the initial symptom is less common. F. Dural sinus hypertension can produce elevated ICP by impeding cerebral venous drainage.

questions.explanation: Proptosis (especially pulsatile) is frequent with carotid-cavernous DAVFs. Pulse-synchronous tinnitus is nearly always exacerbated by a Valsalva maneuver. Dural sinus hypertension can produce elevated ICP by impeding cerebral venous drainage and by impairing the function of the arachnoid granulations (which can also lead to hydrocephalus).

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Clinical features, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Pulsatile tinnitus is the most common initial symptom.
answers.B: Tinnitus occurs because of recruitment of arterial feeders by the DAVF and its close proximity to the middle ear.
answers.C: A bruit can often be auscultated over the cranium.
answers.D: Compression of the carotid artery may result in a reduction in bruit intensity.
answers.E: A change in a bruit (either worsening or disappearance) confirms complete healing.

questions.explanation: Change in a bruit (either worsening or disappearance) should prompts restudy. Pulsatile tinnitus is the most common initial symptom and is frequently associated with high-flow fistulas in the transverse sinus/sigmoid location. Compression of the carotid artery and jugular vein or occipital artery may result in a reduction in bruit intensity and provide a clue to the diagnosis.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Findings on CT are often normal.
answers.B: If the fistula drains to cortical veins, contrast-enhanced CT may demonstrate serpiginous enhancement.
answers.C: CT can miss DAVF but not the MRI.
answers.D: MRI can characterize the anatomy and areas of ischemia and chronic hemorrhage.
answers.E: Evidence of dilated cortical veins in MRI may suggest a DAVF with venous hypertension.

questions.explanation: Both MRI and CT can miss DAVF, especially if small or if the DAVF drains into the ipsilateral venous sinus. Findings on CT are often normal, although it is the most sensitive in evaluating acute subarachnoid, subdural, or intraparenchymal blood.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Angiography is the “gold standard” for diagnosis and delineation of the details of the arterial supply and venous drainage.
answers.B: Premature appearance during early arterial phase of a venous structure within or adjacent to dura mater is characteristic.
answers.C: The pattern of venous drainage is the most critical factor.
answers.D: As a rule, lesions with retrograde flow in the cortical veins are high risk for bleeding or intracranial hypertension.
answers.E: Injection includes internal carotid arteries only.

questions.explanation: Injection must include the vertebral and internal and external carotid arteries because DAVF may be overlooked with conventional studies alone.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Borden classification, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type I fistulas have anterograde drainage into a dural venous sinus or meningeal vein.
answers.B: Type I fistulas are benign, often asymptomatic or characterized by a cranial bruit.
answers.C: Type I fistulas have a high rate of spontaneous remission and can be observed.
answers.D: If conservative treatment is chosen, patients are advised to increase the doses of antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents.
answers.E: Compression therapy is seldom used currently.

questions.explanation: If conservative treatment is chosen, patients are advised to avoid antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, if possible, to prevent interference with spontaneous thrombosis of the DAVF. Borden type I DAVFs have a high rate of spontaneous remission and can be observed, especially since they may spontaneously thrombose, which has been noted with cavernous sinus DAVFs. Compression therapy is seldom used currently, except in patients with Borden type I fistulas as a possible first step before neuroendovascular therapy. Compression of the ipsilateral carotid or occipital artery (if the latter vessel is a known feeder to the fistula) is performed for 30 minutes at a time, three times a day. If compression of the carotid artery is chosen, patients are instructed to use the contralateral arm. In 25 % of simple DAVFs of the transverse/sigmoid sinuses supplied by the occipital artery, compression of the occipital artery results in complete thrombosis of the DAVF within several weeks. The Borden classification system stratifies lesions on the basis of the site of venous drainage and the presence or absence of cortical venous drainage. v Borden classification Type I: Drainage into a meningeal vein, spinal epidural veins, or into a dural venous sinus Normal anterograde flow in both the draining veins and other veins draining into the system Usually have benign clinical behavior with a favorable natural history Equivalent to Cognard type I and IIa Type II: Drainage into meningeal veins, spinal epidural veins, or into a dural venous sinus Retrograde flow into the normal subarachnoid veins It may present with hemorrhage due to venous hypertension Equivalent to Cognard types IIb and IIa+b Type III: Direct drainage into subarachnoid veins or into an isolated segment of the venous sinus Retrograde flow into the normal cortical veins Results from a thrombosis on either side of the dural sinus segment and will cause venous hypertension with a risk of hemorrhage Equivalent to Cognard types III, IV, and V v According to this classification, these lesions are further subclassified into type a (single hole) or type b (multiple hole) fistulas.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Borden classification, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type III fistulas have both anterograde venous sinus drainage and retrograde drainage into subarachnoid veins.
answers.B: In type III fistulas, the venous sinus is always closed.
answers.C: In type III fistulas, high-flow venopathy causes reversal of flow into the arterialized leptomeningeal veins.
answers.D: Type III fistulas have exclusive retrograde drainage into arterialized subarachnoid veins at/or on the wall of dural venous sinuses.
answers.E: In type III fistulas, when the sinus is patent, the point of the fistula can be located between the meningeal artery and leptomeningeal vein.

questions.explanation: In type III fistulas, the venous sinus may be patent but largely defunctionalized because of high-flow venopathy causing reversal of flow into arterialized leptomeningeal veins. In type III fistulas, when the sinus is patent, the point of the fistula is located either between the meningeal artery and leptomeningeal vein or between the meningeal artery and a segment of arterialized dural venous sinus that is thrombosed at either end or somehow isolated from the rest of the sinus, thereby causing reversal of drainage into leptomeningeal veins.

questions.question: DAVFs Cognard classification, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type I fistulas, located in the main sinus, with antegrade flow
answers.B: Type II fistulas, in the main sinus, with reflux into the sinus, cortical veins, or both
answers.C: Type III fistulas with direct cortical venous drainage with venous ectasia
answers.D: Type IV fistulas with direct cortical venous drainage with venous ectasia
answers.E: Type V fistulas with spinal venous drainage

questions.explanation: Type III with direct cortical venous drainage without venous ectasia Type II fistulas, in the main sinus, with reflux into the sinus (IIa), cortical veins (IIb), or both (IIa+b) The Cognard classification is based on angiographic patterns and is generally more applicable to DAVFs involving the transverse sinus. The Cognard classification divides dural arteriovenous fistulas into 5 types according to the following features: Location of fistula Presence of cortical venous drainage Direction of flow Presence of venous ectasia Cognard classification system: Type I: –– Confined to sinus –– Antegrade flow –– No cortical venous drainage/reflux Type II: –– IIa: -- Confined to sinus -- Retrograde flow (reflux) into sinus -- No cortical venous drainage/reflux –– IIb: -- Drains into sinus with reflux into cortical veins -- Antegrade flow –– IIa+b: -- Drains into sinus with reflux into cortical veins -- Retrograde flow Type III: –– Drains directly into cortical veins (not into sinus) drainage (40 % hemorrhage) Type IV: –– Drains directly into cortical veins (not into sinus) drainage with venous ectasia (65 % hemorrhage) Type V: –– Spinal perimedullary venous drainage associated with progressive myelopathy

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Indications for intervention include neurologic dysfunction, hemorrhage, and refractory symptoms.
answers.B: For the treatment to be complete, external carotid injections must demonstrate no abnormal AV shunting.
answers.C: Most DAVFs are better treated endovascularly.
answers.D: Placement copious dural tack-up sutures should be avoided as it predisposes to subdural hematoma.
answers.E: The use of the craniotome is discouraged, as a sinus or venous laceration could produce a fatal hemorrhage.

questions.explanation: Extra care is taken to place copious dural tack-up sutures to obliterate the epidural space which is abnormally vascular. Most DAVFs are better treated endovascularly; however, ethmoidal DAVFs are probably best treated microsurgically.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Treatment modalities for DAVFs include resection, embolization, and radiosurgery.
answers.B: Radiosurgery should be reserved for benign DAVFs that have failed other treatments.
answers.C: Radiosurgery is expected to cause obliteration of DAVFs 1–3 years after the procedure
answers.D: Typically, radiosurgery is performed after embolization.
answers.E: Radiosurgery must ensure that the entire fistula is included in the irradiated volume.

questions.explanation: Typically, radiosurgery is performed before any embolization to ensure that the entire fistula is included in the irradiated volume.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Currently, initial treatment of most DAVFs involves endovascular techniques.
answers.B: DAVFs of the tentorium are traditionally difficult to obliterate endovascularly.
answers.C: DAVFs of the tentorium have multiple small feeding arteries, which are hard to visualize and often originate off the ICAs.
answers.D: Trans-arterial embolization reduces flow through the fistula and can produce complete thrombosis of the DAVF 60 % of the time.
answers.E: Transvenous treatment is appropriate for a Cognard type III fistula, in which there is drainage into the sinus and then reflux into a cortical vein.

questions.explanation: Transvenous treatment is appropriate for a Cognard type IIb fistula, in which there is drainage into the sinus and then reflux into a cortical vein. But it is not appropriate for a Cognard type III fistula, in which there is drainage into a cortical vein and then the sinus. Transvenous embolization has been advocated as the preferred endovascular treatment route because of higher occlusion rates, fewer complications, and a lower rate of recanalization than with trans-arterial embolization. In the latter case, transvenous occlusion of the sinus blocks eventual venous egress, thus further elevating pressure in the arterialized subarachnoid vein. Although generally viewed as incomplete treatment, trans-arterial embolization to reduce flow through the fistula has been reported to produce complete thrombosis of the DAVF 60 % of the time.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: DAVFs Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Microsurgery is the primary modality of treatment for persistent cortical venous drainage following maximal endovascular therapy.
answers.B: Arterial feeders are coagulated and the leptomeningeal arterialized veins are then occluded and divided as close to their dural origin as possible.
answers.C: DAVFs occur more common in children, and when they do they tend to be simple.
answers.D: May be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.
answers.E: Cerebral aneurysms can be associated with DAVFs, especially those located in the anterior cranial fossa and the convexities.

questions.explanation: While congenital DAVFs may rarely occur in children and are typically more complex than adult DAVFs, the majority of adult DAVFs are considered to be acquired idiopathic lesions. The approach to pediatric patients with congenital DAVFs and congestive heart failure involves diminution of flow to permit survival and growth, usually by trans-arterial or mixed trans-arterial/transvenous techniques. If residual DAVF is present, cure is attempted at a later date (3 to 6 months of age). DAVFs occur rarely in children, and when they do they tend to be complex and bilateral. DAVFs may be associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, fibromuscular dysplasia, or neurofibromatosis type 1.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula

answers.C: Never caused by sigmoid sinus occlusion.
answers.D: The occipital artery is the dominant feeder in most cases.
answers.E: Treatment is recommended for all symptomatic transverse-sigmoid sinuses.

Nearly half of these patients had a cranial bruit because of proximity of the draining sinus to the middle ear. Treatment is recommended for all symptomatic transverse-sigmoid sinuses; transvenous embolization is the favored approach, if technically feasible.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: Carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF) Definition, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: An abnormal communication between the ICA or one of its branches or the ECA and the cavernous sinus (CS).
answers.B: The most common cause for the development of CCFs is trauma.
answers.C: The most common complications associated with CCFs involve the ocular findings.
answers.D: Usually CCF occurs in infancy.
answers.E: The two main trunks of the cavernous ICA are commonly implicated in CCFs.

questions.explanation: Usually CCF occurs in the middle aged, but can occur in childhood or infancy. The two main trunks of the cavernous ICA, both commonly implicated in dural CCFs, are the meningo-hypophyseal trunk (most constant) and the inferolateral trunk.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Cavernous sinus (CS) surgical anatomy, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: CS is an extradurally located sinus.
answers.B: The most constant branch of cavernous ICA is the meningo-hypophyseal trunk.
answers.C: The CS in direct continuity through the clivus with the epidural space surrounding the spine.
answers.D: The inferior hypophyseal artery arises directly from cavernous ICA.
answers.E: There are constant anastomoses between branches of the ICA and the ECA. Although not always angiographically visible.

questions.explanation: The inferior hypophyseal artery arises from the meningo-hypophyseal trunk of the cavernous ICA. Anatomically, cavernous sinus is an extradurally located sinus, whereas other dural sinuses are located between two dural walls in the cranial cavity. CS is an extradural space between the two layers of dura laterally and superiorly and the periosteum of lateral portion of the sphenoid bone inferiorly and medially. The ICA with its dural branches traverses the cavernous sinus along with cranial nerves III, IV, V, and VI. The two main trunks of the cavernous ICA, both commonly implicated in dural CCFs, are the meningo-hypophyseal trunk (most constant) and the inferolateral trunk. The meningo-hypophyseal trunk originates near the posterior genu and gives three branches: (i) the tentorial artery, (ii) the dorsal meningeal (clival) artery, and (iii) the inferior hypophyseal artery. The inferolateral trunk originates laterally near the middle of the horizontal segment, courses over the abducent nerve, supplies the adjacent cavernous sinus dura and cranial nerves, and commonly anastomoses with the maxillary and/or middle meningeal arteries through the artery of the foramen rotundum, the artery of the foramen ovale, and/or the foramen spinosum. McConnell’s capsular arteries are inconstant medial branches to the pituitary originating more anteriorly from the horizontal segment of the cavernous ICA.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Cavernous sinus surgical anatomy, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Cavernous sinus is a single venous cavity.
answers.B: The anterior portion receives ophthalmic veins and the sphenoparietal sinus.
answers.C: Posterior drainage is through the basilar plexus and the petrosal sinuses.
answers.D: Inferolaterally, connections exist through dural veins draining into the pterygoid plexus.
answers.E: The two cavernous sinuses communicate through the anterior and posterior intercavernous sinus forming a circular sinus.

questions.explanation: Cavernous sinus is not a single venous space, but exhibits compartmentalization that contains a plexiform arrangement of the veins. The oculomotor nerve is located within the superior lateral cavernous sinus wall and courses anteriorly just beneath the ACP to enter the orbit through the SOF. The trochlear nerve is also located within the lateral cavernous sinus wall, traveling just beneath and parallel to the oculomotor nerve. The first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) courses several millimeters below the oculomotor and trochlear nerves within the lateral sinus wall, whereas the abducent nerve courses within the cavernous venous compartment between the cavernous segment and V1. Finally, sympathetic fiber bundles course as a plexus along the cavernous and clinoidal ICA, eventually departing the ICA proximal to the dural ring to project into the orbit. Disruption of these fibers can occur from operative manipulation of the clinoidal segment, causing mild postoperative ptosis or miosis without facial anhidrosis.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Types, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type A is direct high-flow shunt between ICA and cavernous sinus.
answers.B: Type B is indirect low-flow shunt from meningeal branches of ICA.
answers.C: Type C is indirect low-flow shunt from meningeal branches of ECA.
answers.D: Type D is indirect low-flow shunt from meningeal branches of both ICA and ECA.

questions.explanation: Type A is the most common type. Type D is the most common low flow. They are based on angiographic features (high-flow and low-flow fistulas), mechanism of onset (spontaneous and traumatic), morphology, and angioarchitecture (direct and indirect fistulas). CCF are divided by Barrow classification into direct (type A) and indirect (types B–D) based on arterial supply. Direct (type A) CCF can be subdivided into: A1, direct CCF only or A2, direct CCF with an aneurysm. Type B is extremely rare. answers.E: Traumatic CCFs are more common after penetrating head injury.

answers.E: Indirect CCFs generally have a more gradual onset and milder presentation than direct.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula

answers.E: Spontaneous CCFs may have a male predominance.
