questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Clinical features, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Ocular and/or cranial bruit.
answers.B: If the intraocular pressure is very high, the bruit may not be heard.
answers.C: Diplopia is most commonly due to oculomotor nerve palsy.
answers.D: Ophthalmoplegia is usually unilateral.
answers.E: Secondary open-angle glaucoma.

questions.explanation: Diplopia is most commonly due to abducent nerve palsy. Deterioration of visual acuity may be due to hypoxic retinopathy as a result of reduced arterial pressure and increased venous pressure and increased intraocular pressure. Neovascularization of the iris or retina can also occur. Ophthalmoplegia (usually unilateral, but may present initially as bilateral or may progress to bilateral). CCF also may show central retinal vein occlusion → secondary open-angle glaucoma. The bruit disappears on compression of the carotid in the neck.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Clinical features, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Posteriorly placed fistulas mostly have a significant exophthalmic component.
answers.B: Life-threatening epistaxis is not uncommon with a traumatic direct CCF.
answers.C: ICH can occur with both direct and indirect fistulas associated with retrograde cortical venous drainage.
answers.D: ICH in the setting of a direct CCF frequently portends a poor prognosis.
answers.E: CCFs rarely cause SAH.

questions.explanation: Anteriorly placed fistulas mostly have a significant exophthalmic component. Posterior placed fistulas often have contralateral involvement. Epistaxis, even life-threatening epistaxis, is not uncommon with a traumatic direct CCF and can occur weeks after the trauma. The CCFs that drain posteriorly into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses are usually asymptomatic. Those which drain into supratentorial cortical or posterior fossa veins often present as intracerebral hemorrhage due to rupture of arterialized veins. Those which drain into pterygoid plexus of veins may be asymptomatic or cause pain in the maxillary or mandibular area. ICH in the setting of a direct CCF frequently portends a poor prognosis with a high risk for short-term rehemorrhage.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The serpiginous and engorged superior ophthalmic vein is common sign in CT and MRI.
answers.B: T2WI coronal helps to differentiate superior ophthalmic vein from rectus muscles.
answers.C: The engorged superior ophthalmic vein sign is not present in cavernous meningioma.
answers.D: CT and MRI may also help to study the extent of skull fracture in traumatic CCFs.
answers.E: CT and MRI may show an enlarged cavernous sinus with a convex shape to the lateral wall.

questions.explanation: Serpiginous and engorged intraocular vessels especially the superior ophthalmic vein (best seen on T2WI coronal, helps to differentiate from rectus muscles). However, this sign may also be present in orbital pseudotumor, cavernous meningioma and Grave’s ophthalmopathy. CT and MRI show enlarged superior ophthalmic vein (usually > 4 mm), enlarged muscles, and enlarged cavernous sinus with a convex shape to the lateral wall may suggest a CCF. In MRI the CCF may appear as Caput medusa (engorged, serpiginous intraocular vessels) on T2.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The definitive study to diagnose a CCF is digital subtraction angiography.
answers.B: Huber maneuver of angiography helps to identify lower extent of fistula.
answers.C: Mehringer-Hieshima maneuver of angiography includes injecting the affected ICA while gently compressing the CCA of the neck.
answers.D: Selective injection of the external carotid system is important to define the supply and angioarchitecture of indirect CCFs.
answers.E: Low-flow indirect CCFs may not be visualized on CCA injections only.

questions.explanation: Huber maneuver of angiography: lateral view, inject vertebral artery and manually compress affected carotid. Helps identify upper extent of fistula, multiple fistulous openings, and complete transection of ICA. The definitive study and gold standard to diagnose a CCF is digital subtraction angiography. Definitive diagnosis is based on catheter angiography, which must include selective injections of both ICAs and ECAs and at least one vertebral artery. Low-flow indirect CCFs may not be visualized on CCA injections only.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Treatment (noninvasive), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Medical management is reserved for treatment of low-risk indirect CCFs with ocular findings.
answers.B: An old-aged patient with Barrow type C fistula would most likely be a candidate for an initial trial of nonoperative treatment.
answers.C: Carotid self-compression therapy can be attempted as a noninvasive treatment in low-risk cases.
answers.D: Manual compression therapy can occlude indirect CCFs in about 75 % of cases.
answers.E: The contralateral hand is used to compress the carotid artery in the neck for brief periods of time several times per day.

questions.explanation: Manual compression therapy can occlude indirect CCFs in about 30 % of cases (20–50 % or 10 to 60 % in some texts), therefore one may observe these as long as visual acuity is stable and intraocular pressure is < 25. Carotid self-compression (manual) therapy to assist with spontaneous thrombosis of the CCFs can be attempted as a noninvasive treatment in low-risk cases. Carotid self-compression is done for 20–30 seconds 4 times per hour for 4 to 6 weeks. Patient is instructed to compress carotid artery on the side of the lesion using contralateral hand (should patient develop cerebral ischemia during compression, contralateral hand likely will be affected, releasing compression). Prism glasses or patching for diplopia, topical medications for increased intraocular pressures, and lubrication to minimize risk of proptosis-related keratopathy.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Treatment (indications for early treatment), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Spontaneous closure from thrombosis of cavernous sinus is unlikely.
answers.B: Bruit.
answers.C: Disfiguring progressive proptosis causing exposure keratopathy.
answers.D: Progressive visual failure.
answers.E: Early filling of cortical veins on angiography.

questions.explanation: Intolerable bruit. Other indications for early treatment of CCFs are glaucoma, intolerable headache, diplopia, SAH, ICH, or extension into air sinus. Symptomatic high-flow CCFs rarely resolve spontaneously, and urgent treatment is usually indicated. Spontaneous closure from thrombosis of cavernous sinus is unlikely (as in trauma, high flow). Treatment is usually in the form of endovascular embolization or trapping between surgically placed clips.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The long-term occlusion rate for endovascular treatment of CCFs is 76–100 %.
answers.B: A direct CCF should be considered for endovascular treatment via trans-arterial and/or transvenous approach.
answers.C: Indirect CCFs that fail conservative treatment should be considered for endovascular treatment.
answers.D: Endovascular treatment is necessary if the parent artery is damaged.
answers.E: Surgery may involve ligation of the common or internal carotid artery if embolization fails.

questions.explanation: Surgical treatment can be necessary if the parent artery is particularly damaged and concern exists regarding catheterization of a disrupted vessel, in which case trapping of the damaged segment and the fistula is a valid option.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Endovascular treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Onyx has become the mainstay of treatment of direct CCFs.
answers.B: Routes include transvenous via superior ophthalmic vein or through petrosal sinus to cavernous sinus.
answers.C: Routes include trans-arterial through ICA or ECA.
answers.D: Trans-arterial embolization is reserved for ruptured cavernous ICA aneurysms in direct CCFs.
answers.E: Trans-arterial embolization is reserved for ruptured meningeal feeders of the ECA in indirect CCFs.

questions.explanation: Detachable coils have become the mainstay of treatment of direct CCFs. Unlike coils, which may further compartmentalize the CS, onyx tends to more fully obliterate the fistulous connection. The main advantage of detachable coils is their ability to be retrieved in the event of inadequate placement. A trans-arterial approach to indirect CCFs can be used when adequate supply from the external carotid branches exists. Routes available include trans-arterial through ICA or ECA (useful only for dural fistulas). If trans-arterial embolization fails (e.g., wide aneurysm neck), the carotid artery may be occluded on either side of fistula to trap it (sacrifices carotid artery, therefore test occlusion must be done first to determine if patient can tolerate this). The distal occlusion needs to be proximal to the ophthalmic artery.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF* Transvenous endovascular treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: TVE has higher success rate than trans-arterial route.
answers.B: TVE should not be used for treatment of Barrow type B CCFs.
answers.C: TVE may be used to treat traumatic direct CCFs or type C or D CCFs as well.
answers.D: TVE can be done via traversing the heart to enter the jugular vein and then pass through the petrosal sinus to cavernous sinus.
answers.E: TVE can be done via supraorbital vein while enters orbit to become superior ophthalmic vein.

questions.explanation: TVE has lower success rate (20 %) than trans-arterial route. Transvenous embolization is the primary treatment of Barrow type B CCFs because of the risk of reflux of embolizate into the ICA. Transvenous via superior ophthalmic vein: must avoid lacerating the vein inside the orbit and avoid distal ligation of the vein without proximal occlusion (shunts even more blood into the eye). In TVE via superior ophthalmic vein, it is best to wait for the vein to become arterialized by the high-flow pressure. The surgeon should strike a balance between packing the sinus enough to occlude the fistula and over packing, which can cause cranial nerve palsies.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF* Radiosurgery treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: An effective treatment of direct CCFs.
answers.B: The drawback is latency time during which there is potential risk for ICH.
answers.C: The rationale for performing embolization after radiosurgery is to allow adequate coverage of the fistulous nidus without having it obscured by the embolization.
answers.D: Trans-arterial particle embolization can decrease the flow to lesion while radiosurgery takes effect.
answers.E: With combined radiosurgery and embolization, chemosis and proptosis improved in 94 %.

questions.explanation: Radiosurgery is an effective treatment of low-flow indirect CCFs. The drawback of radiosurgery is the latency time during which patients continue to be exposed to the symptoms and the potential for intracranial hemorrhage. With combined radiosurgery and embolization strategy, chemosis and proptosis were improved in 94 % and 88 % experienced resolution of their visual symptoms.

questions.chapter_title: Dural Arteriovenous Fistula and Carotid-Cavernous Fistula
questions.question: CCF Morbidity and mortality, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Mortality associated with CCFs is due to retrograde cortical drainage resulting in venous congestion and hemorrhages.
answers.B: Complication rate is up to 10 % with multimodality endovascular treatment.
answers.C: Complication rate is generally higher for indirect CCFs.
answers.D: Paradoxical aggravation of the ocular symptoms is uncommon.
answers.E: Recurrence rate of CCF in general is 1–4 %.

questions.explanation: Complication rates are generally higher for direct CCFs. Following treatment, complication rates are up to 10 % with multimodality endovascular treatment. Paradoxical aggravation of the ocular symptoms is uncommon (3 %) and probably related to the effects of CS thrombosis or mass effect from the embolizing material. Up to a third of patients show worsening of preexisting or new extraocular motility deficits after detachable balloon treatment. Often due to the compression of the sixth cranial nerve running in the CS, usually transient.

questions.question: Cavernoma (cavernous malformation, cavernous hemangioma, or cavernous angioma) The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: A low-flow well-circumscribed, benign vascular hamartoma.
answers.B: Cavernomas consist of irregular thick- and thin-walled sinusoidal vascular channels located within the brain but no arteries.
answers.C: Cavernomas comprise 9 % of CNS vascular malformations.
answers.D: Cavernomas are mainly supratentorial.
answers.E: Cavernomas are the only vascular malformation with intervening neural parenchyma.

questions.explanation: The only vascular malformation without intervening neural parenchyma. A low-flow well-circumscribed, benign vascular hamartoma consisting of irregular thick- and thinwalled sinusoidal channels located within the brain but no arteries.

questions.question: Cavernomas Location, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Two-thirds are supratentorial.
answers.B: Common in the frontal or temporal lobes.
answers.C: 4–35 % of cavernomas in the brainstem.
answers.D: 5–10 % of cavernomas in the basal ganglia.
answers.E: Associated with developmental venous anomaly (DVA) that should be resected also.

questions.explanation: Associated with DVA (represents venous outflow and should be preserved). 4–35 % of cavernomas in the brainstem (commonly in the pons).

questions.question: Cavernoma Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Caverns are filled with blood in various stages of thrombus formation, organization, and dissolution and may calcify.
answers.B: Cavernoma’s gross appearance resembles a mulberry.
answers.C: Cavernoma is sometimes called “the hemorrhoid of the brain.”
answers.D: Cavernoma has abnormally hypertrophied smooth muscle layer.
answers.E: Two types: sporadic and hereditary (autosomal dominant).

questions.explanation: Smooth muscle layer is absent or minimum. Light microscopy: stains for von Willebrand’s factor. EM: shows abnormal gapping of the tight junctions between endothelial cells (may permit leakage of blood).

questions.question: Cavernoma* Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Cystic variant of cavernoma occurs more commonly in the posterior fossa.
answers.B: Dural-based variant of cavernoma occurs more commonly in the parasellar area.
answers.C: Hemangioma calcificans variant of cavernoma occurs more in the temporal lobe.
answers.D: Cavernomas are very rarely multiple.
answers.E: Previous radiotherapy appears to be a risk factor.

questions.explanation: Cavernomas are multiple in less than 50 %. Previous radiotherapy appears to be a risk factor especially for spinal cavernomas.

questions.question: Cavernoma Presentation, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The most common presentation is seizures and progressive neurologic deficit.
answers.B: 20 % of cavernomas presented with hemorrhage.
answers.C: Hemorrhage appears to be higher in females.
answers.D: Hemorrhage is always fatal.
answers.E: Cavernoma may rarely present with hydrocephalus or as in incidental finding.

questions.explanation: Hemorrhage risk is difficult to predict, but rarely fatal. The common presentations are seizures (60 %), progressive neurologic deficit (50 %), hemorrhage (20 %) (usually intraparenchymal), hydrocephalus, or as in incidental finding.

questions.question: Cavernoma Risk factors for hemorrhage, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The size of the cavernoma (>1 cm)
answers.B: Female gender and pregnancy
answers.C: Prior symptomatic bleed
answers.D: Age more than 35 years
answers.E: Deep location of the lesion

questions.explanation: Age less than 35 years is also a risk factor for hemorrhage.

questions.question: Cavernoma Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: CT scan is sensitive but not specific.
answers.B: Gradient-echo T2WI MRI is the most sensitive test.
answers.C: In MRI, the mixed signal core with low-signal rim described as “popcorn” pattern is pathognomonic.
answers.D: Angiography is highly sensitive for cavernomas.
answers.E: The diagnosis is strongly suggested by finding multiple lesions with a positive family history.

questions.explanation: Angiography for cavernomas is usually negative (usually angiographically occult). CT scan is sensitive but not specific. May overlap with low-grade tumors, hemorrhages, and granulomas. Diffusion tensor imaging/white matter tractography and preop 3D-constructive interference in steady-state (CISS) MRI may improve localization, approach, and post-op outcomes.

questions.question: Cavernoma* Radiology, Zabramski classification, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Type I: subacute hemorrhage
answers.B: Type II: classic “popcorn ball” lesion
answers.C: Type III: chronic hemorrhage
answers.D: Type IV: multiple punctate micro-hemorrhages
answers.E: Type I is the most common type

questions.explanation: Type II is the most common type. The Zabramski classification is a radiological classification of cerebral cavernomas malformations. Zabramski classification of cavernomas: Type I: subacute hemorrhage –– T1: hyperintense –– T2: hypo- or hyperintense Type II: most common type—classic “popcorn” lesion –– T1: mixed signal intensity centrally –– T2: mixed signal intensity centrally –– Low-signal rim with blooming on T2 sequences Type III: chronic hemorrhage –– T1: hypointense to isointense centrally –– T2: hypointense centrally –– Low-signal rim with blooming on T2 sequences Type IV: multiple punctate micro-hemorrhages –– T1: difficult to identify –– T2: difficult to identify –– T2 gradient echo: “black dots” with blooming –– Difficult to distinguish from small capillary telangiectasias

questions.question: Cavernoma Indications of surgery, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Accessible lesions with focal deficit
answers.B: Less accessible lesions that repeatedly bleed with progressive neurologic deterioration may be considered for excision
answers.C: Brainstem cavernomas that have not bled
answers.D: Symptomatic hemorrhage
answers.E: New onset seizures or difficult to manage seizures

questions.explanation: Surgery is almost never indicated for brainstem cavernomas that have not bled.

questions.question: Cavernoma Management, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Asymptomatic, incidentally discovered cavernomas should be managed expectantly.
answers.B: Expectant management is usually with serial imaging studies for about 2–3 years.
answers.C: Never remove the hemosiderin-stained brain immediately surrounding the cavernoma.
answers.D: Goal of surgery is complete removal of the malformation.
answers.E: Piecemeal excision is an option, especially in brainstem cavernomas.

questions.explanation: For supratentorial cavernomas presenting with seizures, it is desirable to also remove the hemosiderin-stained brain immediately surrounding the cavernoma. Expectant management is usually with serial imaging studies for about 2–3 years (to rule out frequent subclinical bleeds).

questions.question: Cavernoma Management, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: If an associated venous angioma is found, it should not be removed.
answers.B: Biopsy to verify the diagnosis is usually indicated.
answers.C: Stereotactic radiosurgery is not an alternative to surgery.
answers.D: Outcome is worse with surgery through the floor of the fourth ventricle than with a lateral approach.
answers.E: Worsening of neurologic outcome is more in deep cavernoma resections than in superficial.

questions.explanation: Since the radiographic appearance is almost pathognomonic, biopsy to verify the diagnosis is rarely appropriate. If an associated venous angioma is found, it should not be removed as they represent the venous drainage of the area. Worsening of neurologic outcome was 9 % vs. 29 % in superficial vs. deep brainstem cavernoma resections, respectively. Developmental Venous Anomaly 4.1

questions.question: DVA, developmental venous anomaly or venous malformation or venous angioma General, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: DVA is not a pathologic lesion, but a normal variant.
answers.B: DVA has several prominent deep parenchymal veins that drain a normal part of the brain and then drain into an unusually large draining vein.
answers.C: Pathologic characteristics consist of anomalous veins separated by normal brain tissue.
answers.D: DVAs are high-flow, high-pressure lesions.
answers.E: There is an equal prevalence in men and women.

questions.explanation: DVAs are low-flow, low-pressure lesions.

questions.question: DVA Presentation, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: DVAs are the most common intracranial vascular malformation in autopsy.
answers.B: DVAs are the least common form encountered in surgical series.
answers.C: Most are clinically silent.
answers.D: DVAs are most commonly seen in the occipital lobe.
answers.E: Most common in regions supplied by the MCA.

questions.explanation: DVAs are commonly seen in the frontal lobe or in the cerebellum. The diagnosis is typically made in the third decade. Rarely cause seizures and even less frequently hemorrhage may occur. Most common in regions supplied by the MCA or in the region of vein of Galen.

questions.question: DVA Radiology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The angiographic and MRI appearance is pathognomonic resembling the “head of Medusa.”
answers.B: The “head of Medusa” sign has other names like a hydra or a spider.
answers.C: In angiography, the DVA appears as a long draining vein (longer than a normal vein).
answers.D: In arterial phase of angiography, the DVA should show no AV shunting.
answers.E: In MRI, DVAs are best visualized on T2-weighted images.

questions.explanation: They are best visualized on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images. The “head of Medusa” is a Greek mythological figure which refers to a woman’s hair that is made of serpents. Other angiographic descriptive terms include spokes of a wheel, an umbrella, a mushroom, or a sunburst or starburst. In arterial phase of angiography, the DVA should show no AV shunting (characteristic of AVM).

questions.question: DVA Management, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: In general, DVAs should not be treated as they are the venous drainage of the brain in that vicinity.
answers.B: If symptoms are present, look for an associated cavernous malformation.
answers.C: If surgery is indicated for associated cavernous malformations, the DVA should be left alone.
answers.D: Surgery for the DVA itself is reserved only for documented bleeding or for intractable seizures definitely attributed to the lesion.
answers.E: SRS and endovascular approach are alternative treatment options for DVAs.

questions.explanation: SRS is of no benefit for venous angioma, and it is not accessible by an endovascular approach. Because DVAs drain normal brain parenchyma, treatment may result in devastating venous infarcts. Coexistence of a cavernoma with a venous angioma occurs in about 8 % of cases. Multiple DVAs are reported to be more associated with cavernoma. Capillary Telangiectasia 4.2

questions.question: Capillary telangiectasia (capillary malformation) Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Capillary telangiectasia is a vascular malformation composed of dilated capillaries.
answers.B: Capillary telangiectasia contains normal intervening neural tissue.
answers.C: The normal intervening neural tissue is the only and the most important feature that distinguishes it from cavernomas.
answers.D: Microscopically, they consist of ectatic individual vessels with thin capillary walls that course among normal architectural elements.
answers.E: Capillary telangiectasias have adjacent gliosis or hemosiderin deposition.

questions.explanation: Capillary telangiectasias are characterized by the absence of adjacent gliosis or hemosiderin deposition.

questions.question: Capillary telangiectasia The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The most commonly detected intracranial vascular malformation in autopsy.
answers.B: Capillary telangiectasias are rarely symptomatic.
answers.C: They are most often solitary.
answers.D: Capillary telangiectasias are usually multiple if associated with ataxia-telangiectasia syndrome.
answers.E: Most commonly located in the pons.

questions.explanation: Capillary telangiectasia is second most commonly detected vascular malformation in autopsy, while DVA is the most common intracranial vascular malformation in autopsy. They are most often solitary; however, multiple lesions are found in sporadic or syndromic vascular malformations such as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, or Wyburn-Mason syndrome. Are most commonly located in the pons, but may occur elsewhere in the CNS, as well as in other organs.

questions.question: Brain capillary telangiectasia The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The lack of a mass effect or increased T2 signal argues against other pathology.
answers.B: Capillary telangiectasia is a histopathological diagnosis rather than a radiologic one.
answers.C: Capillary telangiectasias are always diagnosed angiographically.
answers.D: The only vascular malformation that is composed of sacs of stagnant blood with deoxyhemoglobin.
answers.E: No further treatments are currently advised

questions.explanation: Capillary telangiectasias are classified as “angiographically occult” lesions. The only vascular malformation that is composed of sacs of stagnant blood with deoxyhemoglobin thus exhibit susceptibility dephasing, which is evident only on gradient-echo images. Brain capillary telangiectasias are most often discovered in the third and fourth decades of life. These lesions are usually silent on CT and angiography, but have characteristic presentations on contrast-enhanced MRI studies, specifically demonstrating susceptibility to gradient-echo sequences and “brush”- or “stipple”-like enhancement interspersed among normal brain parenchyma. Diagnosis is based primarily on radiographic findings, and no further treatments are currently advised. Follow-up imaging may be obtained to ensure stability and to confirm the diagnosis. Angiographically Occult (or Cryptic) Vascular 4.3 Malformations (AOVMs)

questions.question: AOVMs, not visualized due to the following factors The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Transiently occult AVMs due to destruction or compression by hematoma or edema
answers.B: Transiently occult AVMs due to late filling
answers.C: All AVMs
answers.D: Intraluminal thrombosis because of stagnation or sluggish flow
answers.E: Changes in blood vessels as spasm or dysplastic changes

questions.explanation: Only micro-AVM Intraluminal thrombosis because of stagnation or sluggish or turbulent flow Changes in blood vessels, e.g., fibrosis, spasm, placation, or dysplastic changes

questions.question: AOVMs The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Incidence of AOVM has been estimated as 50 % of cerebrovascular malformations.
answers.B: Abnormal arteriovenous connections histologically but are not revealed by catheter angiography.
answers.C: AOVM usually does not demonstrate mass effect or surrounding edema.
answers.D: The risk of hemorrhage from a cryptic vascular malformation is very low.
answers.E: This appears to be more common in lesions located within the posterior fossa.

questions.explanation: Incidence of AOVM has been estimated as 10 % of cerebrovascular malformations. The risk of hemorrhage from a cryptic vascular malformation is around 0.25 % per year. AOVM most often may be discovered incidentally or present with seizures or headache. Less commonly they may present with progressive neurologic symptoms.

questions.question: AOVMs The FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Many lesions have large patent vessels at surgery in spite of negative angiography.
answers.B: The presence of a histologically definable arterial component separates true occult AVMs from other occult vascular malformations.
answers.C: AVMs are the most common AOVM.
answers.D: Most of DVAs are angiographically occult.
answers.E: Cavernomas are most commonly an AOVM.

questions.explanation: Most of DVAs are not angiographically occult. Many lesions have large patent vessels at surgery in spite of negative angiography, but other imaging modalities (i.e., CT, MRI) may be able to reveal these lesions. Mixed or unclassified angiomas account for 11 % of AOVM.

questions.question: VGAMs Definition, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The anatomic landmark of a VGAM is the presence of multiple arteriovenous shunts draining into a dilated median prosencephalic vein.
answers.B: True VGAM are mainly fed from the choroidal and other surrounding arteries.
answers.C: Are defined as arteriovenous fistulas in the choroid fissure supplied by the choroidal arteries and draining to the dilated median prosencephalic vein.
answers.D: Are defined as arteriovenous fistulas in the wall of a persistent embryonic vascular channel called the median prosencephalic vein.
answers.E: The median prosencephalic vein is an embryonic vessel normally present at the adult stage.

questions.explanation: The median prosencephalic vein is an embryonic vessel normally absent at the adult stage.

questions.question: VGAMs Definition, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Represent only 1 % of all cerebral vascular malformations.
answers.B: Represent up to 30 % of all pediatric vascular malformations.
answers.C: The median prosencephalic vein develops at the sixth week of gestation.
answers.D: The median prosencephalic vein of Markowski usually regresses during the 11th week of gestation.
answers.E: The vein of Galen is formed by the confluence of the internal cerebral veins only.

questions.explanation: The vein of Galen is formed by the confluence of the internal cerebral veins and the basal vein of Rosenthal. The median prosencephalic vein of Markowski usually regresses during the 11th week of gestation, and by 3 months of gestation, the posterior part of it joins the internal cerebral veins and basal veins to form the vein of Galen.

questions.question: Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations (VGAMs) Anatomy, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The vein of Galen lies in the suprasellar cistern.
answers.B: The vein of Galen drains the thalamus.
answers.C: The vein of Galen drains the occipital lobes.
answers.D: The vein of Galen drains the medial temporal lobes.
answers.E: The vein of Galen drains the superior cerebellar vermis.

questions.explanation: The vein of Galen lies in the quadrigeminal cistern. The structures drained by the vein of Galen include the thalamus, the medial temporal lobes, the occipital lobes, and the superior cerebellar vermis.

questions.question: VGAMs Anatomy, vein of Galen normal venous tributaries, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Veins from the ambient cistern
answers.B: Veins from the corpus callosum cistern
answers.C: Veins from the superior cerebellar cistern
answers.D: Veins from the sylvian cistern
answers.E: Veins from the velum interpositum cistern

questions.explanation: The vein of Galen receives veins from the ambient, corpus callosum and superior cerebellar cistern, as well as the velum interpositum cistern.

questions.question: VGAMs Anatomy, VGAM main arterial feeders, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The anterior choroidal arteries
answers.B: The posterior choroidal arteries
answers.C: The vertebral arteries
answers.D: The pericallosal arteries
answers.E: The thalamoperforating arteries

questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries are not usual feeders for VGAM although it usually receives feeders from both anterior and posterior circulations. True VGAM are predictably fed from the choroidal, circumferential mesencephalic, pericallosal, and meningeal arteries.

questions.question: VGAMs Yasargil classification, the FALSE answer is:

questions.explanation: Type III is the most common type. Yasargil classified based on the arterial supply pattern of the malformation. The Yasargil classification is probably the most descriptive one so far proposed, with application toward open neurosurgery, whereas the Lasjaunias system is more applicable to endovascular approaches. Yasargil classification of vein of Galen malformations: Type I: Pure cisternal fistula between pericallosal arteries (anterior or posterior), posterior cerebral artery (P3–P4 and its branches), and the vein of Galen Type II: Fistulous connections between the thalamoperforators (basilar and P1 segment) and the vein of Galen Type III: Mixed form with characteristics of both type I and II lesions (high flow) (the most common type) Type IV: Plexiform (parenchymal) AVM with one or more intrinsic niduses within the mesencephalon or thalamus with draining veins emptying into vein of Galen (also known as secondary type) Type IVA: Pure plexiform nidus in the parenchyma of thalamus Type IVB: Pure plexiform nidus in the parenchyma of mesencephalon Type IVC: Nidus within the parenchyma combined with fistulous cisternal nidus (type I)

questions.question: VGAMs Lasjaunias classification, choroidal type, the FALSE answer is:

answers.B: Choroidal type is the simplest type.
answers.C: Choroidal multiple feeders include thalamoperforating, choroidal, and pericallosal arteries.

answers.E: Lasjaunias choroidal type equals to Yasargil type I.

answers.E: Cardiac failure, if present, is mild and cardiomegaly may be asymptomatic.

questions.explanation: The mural type is associated with more severe dilation of median prosencephalic vein. Lasjaunias proposed an angiographic classification depending on the number and origin of feeding arteries. Lasjaunias classification of vein of Galen malformations: Choroidal type: –– Multiple feeders including thalamoperforating, choroidal, and pericallosal arteries are located in the subarachnoid space in the choroidal fissure. –– Converge on a fistula site at the anterior aspect of median prosencephalic vein. –– Tend to present earlier (neonate) with more severe shunts. –– Clinically, this type is the most severe form of the disease. –– This type of VGAM results in high-output cardiac failure because of multiple high-flow fistulas with less outflow restriction. –– Type I, the choroidal type, is the most common and more complex type. Mural type: –– Fistulae in the subarachnoid space in the wall of the median prosencephalic vein. –– Arterial feeders arise from the collicular or quadrigeminal arteries and/or the posterior choroidal arteries. –– Supply may be unilateral or bilateral. –– Associated with the absence or stenosis of dural sinuses. –– Associated with stenosis at the level of the jugular foramen. –– This type of VGAM presents with fewer fistulas with high outflow restriction. –– Due to the smaller number of fistulas and more outflow obstruction, they are associated with more severe dilation of the median prosencephalic vein and manifest later in infancy as macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, or failure to thrive. Cardiac failure, if present, is mild and cardiomegaly may be asymptomatic. New classification system proposed by Mortazavi et al.: proposed a new classification scoring system combining the previous ones and including the two most important parameters affecting outcomes reported so far: heart failure and age. questions.question: VGAMs Clinical feature, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Neonate presenting with almost always significant high-output cardiac failure.
answers.B: On examination has bulging anterior fontanelle with a bruit on auscultation.
answers.C: Infant presenting with hydrocephalus and/or seizures.
answers.D: Older child or adult presenting with headaches or SAH.
answers.E: The basis for most clinical symptoms is the mass effect.

questions.explanation: The basis for most clinical symptoms is not the mass effect, but rather the shunting of blood through the fistula that produces either cerebral or coronary artery “steal.” Cyanosis is very common and is typically refractory to medical therapy.

answers.D: Persistence of other embryologic sinuses, such as the occipital and marginal sinuses, is often observed in patients with VGAMs.
answers.E: Persisting arterial anomalies such as a limbic arterial ring involving the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries and pericallosal arteries are also frequently present.

questions.explanation: The straight sinus is absent with most VGAMs.

questions.question: VGAMs* Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Is associated with hydrodynamic disorder caused by the intracranial arteriovenous shunting.
answers.B: The hydrodynamic disorder describes a state of disturbed absorption of CSF and venous hypertension.
answers.C: VGMs may be associated with Down syndrome.
answers.D: VGMs may be associated with supernumerary digits, hypospadias.
answers.E: VGMs may be associated with transposition of great vessels, aortic stenosis, and right-sided aortic arch.

questions.explanation: VGMs may be associated with Turner syndrome and blue rubber bleb syndrome not Down syndrome. The hydrodynamic disorder describes a state of disturbed absorption of CSF and venous hypertension caused by the intracranial arteriovenous shunting that occurs in patients with VGAM.

questions.question: VGAMs* Pathology (melting brain syndrome), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Melting brain syndrome describes an advanced stage of the hydrodynamic disorder.
answers.B: Melting brain syndrome is indicative of a poor prognosis.
answers.C: Cerebral blood flow is decreased because of venous hypertension, and the brain parenchyma is acutely destroyed.
answers.D: The ventricular system is enlarged, but intracranial pressure is not elevated.
answers.E: Melting brain syndrome usually occurs in adults.

questions.explanation: Melting brain syndrome can occur in fetuses, neonates, and infants, but it is not observed in adults. Cerebral blood flow is decreased because of venous hypertension, and the brain parenchyma (white matter) is acutely and progressively destroyed. Melting brain syndrome can be associated with all types of AV fistulas, including VGAMs, pial AVMs, and dural sinus malformations. Although it occurs bilaterally and symmetrically, brain atrophy around a pial AVM can be regarded as a focal expression of the same phenomenon.

questions.question: VGAMs Investigations, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Mutations in the RASA 1 gene may be involved in the pathogenesis of VGAM.
answers.B: Contrast CT scan is the gold standard.
answers.C: Brain CT scan may show “ta rget sign.”
answers.D: MRI provides greater details about the ischemic changes occurring in the affected brain.
answers.E: The final diagnosis of the malformation is provided by cerebral angiography.

questions.explanation: Cerebral angiography is the gold standard. CT scan shows the characteristic features, namely, calcification, low-density cystic spaces, and post-contrast enhancement. On CT scan, central thrombus and peripheral circulating blood along the wall of the sac can produce the so-called “target sign.” An MRI scan is more sensitive than a CT scan since it provides better information concerning the malformation and its effects on the surrounding brain. An MRI scan provides greater details about the ischemic changes occurring in the affected brain and also depicts the patency and size of the large arteries, veins, and venous sinus.

questions.question: VGAMs Investigations, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Prenatal ultrasonography shows the characteristic midline tubular anaechoic structure inferior to the thalamus.
answers.B: Prenatal ultrasonography shows “keyhole sign.”
answers.C: Trans-fontanelle ultrasonography shows a hypoechoic midline mass with dilated lateral ventricles.
answers.D: Doppler evaluation is important in differentiating this lesion from other cystic lesions of the brain.
answers.E: VGAMs are the only lesion that clearly displays blood flow within it in Doppler evaluation.

questions.explanation: Prenatal ultrasonography shows the characteristic midline tubular anaechoic structure superior to the thalamus, which is contiguous with the dilated sagittal sinus (comet tail or keyhole sign).

questions.question: VGAMs* Investigations, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Differential diagnoses include arachnoid cyst and quadrigeminal cistern.
answers.B: Differential diagnoses include cavum vergi and cavum septum pellucidum.

answers.E: Serial plasma BNP is helpful as a prognostic indicator.

questions.explanation: Differential diagnosis includes arachnoid cyst, cavum vergi, cavum septum pellucidum, and quadrigeminal cistern. None of these show flow on Doppler evaluation, only the VAGMs show a flow. Monitoring serial plasma BNP provides valuable information regarding the need for additional evaluation or treatment of newborns with CHF and is also helpful as a prognostic indicator.

questions.question: VGAMs Treatment, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Ideally, the initial treatment is conservative.
answers.B: Ideally, the intervention should be delayed until the infant is 5 or 6 months old.
answers.C: If there are clinical signs of an acute deterioration, urgent definitive treatment may be indicated.
answers.D: The cardiac status of the patient usually improves significantly after embolization, even if complete occlusion of the VGAM cannot be achieved.
answers.E: The radiosurgery is never used in VGAMs.

questions.explanation: The radiosurgery can be used and is limited to the last stage of treatment for a small residual in older children. Modalities may include embolization (mainstay), surgery, shunting for hydrocephalus, or a combination therapy. Complete occlusion of the lesion is not the objective at this age because of the increased risk for complications and limitation in the use of contrast material. The goal of medical treatment is to control the cardiac failure so that the baby can tolerate oral feeding and gain weight.

questions.question: VGAMs Treatment of hydrocephaly, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: It is best to avoid ventricular shunting.
answers.B: The aim of the therapy is correcting the basic pathology.
answers.C: The results of most shunting procedures for ventriculomegaly in infants and neonates are excellent.
answers.D: If endovascular treatment is performed after the full development of hydrocephalus, the effect of embolization is usually insufficient.
answers.E: Embolization should be avoided for at least a few days after placement of a ventricular shunt.

questions.explanation: The results of most shunting procedures for ventriculomegaly in infants and neonates are disappointing because intraventricular pressure is invariably low. The aim of the therapy is correcting the basic pathology. This strategy has shown to normalize the head circumference. If endovascular treatment is performed after the full development of hydrocephalus, the effect of embolization is usually insufficient, and third ventriculostomy or a ventricular shunt should then be considered. Embolization should be avoided for at least a few days after placement of a ventricular shunt to avoid the risk for upward cerebellar herniation secondary to a rapid decrease in supratentorial pressure. Although compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius by the VGAM may be present, obstructive hydrocephalus is rare. It is also possible for the ventriculomegaly to progress without increased intracranial pressure because of subependymal atrophy. Third ventriculostomy may be sufficient and more preferable than ventricular shunting for the treatment of hydrocephalus if it is combined with embolization of the VGAM.

answers.B: Development of significant macrocrania or hydrocephalus
answers.C: Recognition of developmental delay
answers.D: Recognition of venous ischemic changes such as calcifications

questions.question: VGAMs* Treatment (endovascular embolization): the FALSE answer is:

answers.B: Transvenous approach is reserved for patients in whom trans-arterial embolization is impossible or unsuccessful.

answers.E: Trans-arterial embolization is most suitable for Yasargil type I, II, or III malformations.

questions.explanation: Trans-arterial embolization is the primary choice of treatment. Transvenous approach is technically easier but is associated with a higher rate of post procedure hemorrhage than is the case with trans-arterial embolization because of the sudden increase in venous back pressure with a patent fistula. The main complication is hemorrhage due to increased venous hypertension which can be avoided by staged procedure.

questions.question: VGAMs* Treatment (endovascular embolization), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: A transumbilical artery approach may be preferable in newborn.
answers.B: For a mural-type VGAM, complete obliteration requires one or two sessions of endovascular treatment.
answers.C: For a choroidal-type VGAM, complete obliteration requires several sessions of endovascular treatment.
answers.D: In most neonates, 20 ml/kg body weight of contrast material is well tolerated.
answers.E: The total amount of contrast material that can be tolerated by a patient depends on the duration of the procedure and urinary output.

questions.explanation: In most neonates, up to 8 mL/kg body weight of contrast material is well tolerated. A transumbilical artery approach is possible for newborn patients and sometimes preferable because of the small size of the femoral artery. For a mural-type VGAM, complete obliteration of the lesion can usually be achieved in one or two sessions of endovascular treatment. For a choroidal-type VGAM, several sessions of staged embolization may be necessary over a period of several years to achieve complete obliteration.

questions.question: VGAMs Treatment (surgery), the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Surgery alone is the best and definitive choice for the treatment of VGAMs.
answers.B: Microsurgery is usually reserved in medically stable patients especially for Yasargil type I.
answers.C: Microsurgery is usually reserved in medically stable patients especially for less complex Yasargil types II and III.
answers.D: The galenic region can surgically be approached by the subtemporal, transcallosal, or transtentorial approaches.
answers.E: The posterior interhemispheric approach is most commonly used to adequately access a vein of Galen malformation and expose the feeding arteries.

questions.explanation: Surgery alone has only a limited adjunctive role for the treatment of VGAMs. A staged approach during the neonatal period, with the use of selective embolization or occlusion of vessels, to reduce the volume of the arteriovenous shunt until the patient is older and better able to tolerate major operation. Types 4A and 4B vein of Galen aneurysms carry significantly higher treatment risk for postoperative death or neurological deficit; direct intraoperative injection of thalamoperforating feeding vessels with acrylic glue can be used on these cases with some success.

questions.question: VGAMs Prognosis, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Typically, patients with VGAMs die from a combination of cerebral and cardiac events.

questions.explanation: Neonates usually succumb to their cardiac insufficiency, while older children and adults usually succumb to the cerebral injury. Untreated VGAMs have a poor prognosis, with neonates having nearly 100 % mortality, and 1–12 month olds having 60 % mortality, 7 % major morbidity, and 21 % being normal.

questions.question: VGAMS* Other types, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Vein of Galen Varix indicates dilation of vein of Galen without the presence of an AV shunt.
answers.B: Vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation in contrast to VGAM: the midline ectatic vein in this group is the true vein of Galen, and it therefore receives drainage from the normal brain, as well as the malformation.
answers.C: Pial AVMs with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation, usually initially manifested in childhood or young adulthood as intracerebral hemorrhage, focal neurological deficit, or seizures.
answers.D: Dural AVMs with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation is an acquired lesion in which AV shunts are located in the wall of the vein of Galen itself.
answers.E: Endovascular treatment is easy and of choice for dural AVMs with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation.

questions.explanation: Dural arteriovenous malformation with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation: endovascular treatment of this type of dural AVM had been difficult because the transvenous approach is often not feasible and there are too many feeders from both the carotid and vertebral arteries for trans-arterial embolization. Dural AVMs with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation is an acquired lesion in which AV shunts are located in the wall of the vein of Galen itself; typical clinical findings are headaches and progressive dementia. Vein of Galen Varix: VGV indicates dilation of the vein of Galen without the presence of an AV shunt and it is usually asymptomatic. Vein of Galen Varix: Two types have been encountered in children. One is transient asymptomatic dilation of the vein of Galen in neonates with cardiac failure from a cause other than VGAM. This dilation is usually noticed on an ultrasound study and disappears in several days after improvement of the cardiac condition. The second type of VGV occurs as an anatomic variation in which venous drainage of the brain converges toward the deep venous system. It is also asymptomatic, but this arrangement of venous drainage may predispose to future venous thrombosis and resultant ischemic symptoms because of the lack of compliance. Pial arteriovenous malformation with vein of Galen aneurysmal dilation: For treatment, transvenous occlusion of the venous dilation in the VGAD is contraindicated because it may produce hemorrhage or venous infarction of the deep cerebral structures as a result of occlusion of the outflow of these veins. Demonstration of trans-mesencephalic feeders by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or angiography confirms the pial nature of the lesion.

questions.question: Moyamoya Disease (MMD) Definition, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: A rare chronic cerebrovascular disease characterized by stenosis-occlusion of the bilateral ICAs at their terminal portion and subsequent development of peculiar moyamoya vasculature at the base of the brain.
answers.B: The term moyamoya means “something hazy, like a puff of smoke.”
answers.C: The term moyamoya describes the characteristic angiographic appearance of abnormally dilated collateral vessels in MMD.
answers.D: An increasingly recognized cause of stroke.
answers.E: MMD is the most common pediatric cerebrovascular disease worldwide.

questions.explanation: MMD including 6 % of all strokes in children. In Japan, it is the most common pediatric cerebrovascular disease. Rare chronic cerebrovascular disease characterized by stenosis-occlusion of the bilateral ICAs at their terminal portion (carotid fork) and the subsequent development of peculiar moyamoya vasculature at the base of the brain. The term moyamoya comes from a Japanese expression for something “hazy just like a puff of cigarette smoke drifting in the air” was first described by Suzuki and Takaku in 1969.

answers.A: To have moyamoya disease, patients usually have bilateral stenosis.

answers.D: Idiopathic cases with no known risk factors have moyamoya syndrome.
answers.E: The term moyamoya, when used alone without the modifier of disease or syndrome, refers to the distinctive findings on arteriography, independent of etiology.

questions.explanation: Individuals with a well-recognized associated condition are categorized as having moyamoya syndrome, whereas idiopathic cases with no known risk factors have moyamoya disease. answers.D: Asian Americans are more than four times as likely to have moyamoya.
answers.E: African Americans are twice as likely to have moyamoya.

Asian Americans are more than four times as likely, African Americans are twice as likely, and Hispanic Americans are half as likely to have moyamoya.

questions.question: MMD Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: In all cases, the process extends to involve the posterior circulation.

answers.C: Pathologic analysis has demonstrated that affected vessels generally do not exhibit arteriosclerotic or inflammatory changes.
answers.D: Pathologic analysis has demonstrated that vessel occlusion results from a combination of both hyperplasia of smooth muscle cells and luminal thrombosis.
answers.E: Occlusion of the anterior circulation occurs simultaneously as characteristic arterial collateral vessels develop at the base of the brain in response to the resultant ischemia.

questions.question: MMD Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: The moyamoya collaterals are dilated perforating arteries believed to be a combination of preexisting and newly developed vessels.

answers.E: Vault moyamoya have abnormally dilated collaterals via the dural arteries.

questions.question: MMD Pathology, the FALSE answer is:

answers.D: The ECA collateral networks providing extracranial (EC)-to-intracranial (IC) anastomoses also develop.
answers.E: The EC-to-IC anastomoses particularly from middle meningeal, ethmoidal, and occipital arteries.

questions.explanation: The moyamoya vessels may harbor aneurysmal dilatations. The moyamoya vessels show increased expression of growth factors.

questions.question: MMD, association, the FALSE answer is:

answers.B: Moyamoya is strongly associated with radiotherapy for pituitary tumors.
answers.C: Moyamoya is associated with Down syndrome.
answers.D: Moyamoya is strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type II.
answers.E: Moyamoya is associated with sickle cell anemia.

questions.explanation: Strong associations exist between moyamoya and radiotherapy of the head or neck (especially for optic gliomas, craniopharyngiomas, and pituitary tumors), Down syndrome, neurofibromatosis type I (with or without hypothalamic-optic pathway tumors), and sickle cell anemia.

questions.question: MMD* Genetics, the FALSE answer is:

answers.A: Moyamoya may be associated with mutation in loci on chromosomes 3.
answers.B: Moyamoya may be associated with mutation in loci on chromosomes 6.
answers.C: Moyamoya may be associated with mutation in loci on chromosomes 8.

answers.E: Moyamoya is strongly associated with haplotype at chromosome 2.

A single haplotype of the RNF213 locus at chromosome 17q is strongly associated with moyamoya disease. Mutation analysis of RNF213 identified a founder mutation present in 95 % of Japanese familial moyamoya disease, 73 % of nonfamilial moyamoya disease, and only 1.4 % of controls.
